notes.definition: The relative atomic mass (Ar) of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.
explanation: Most elements exist naturally as a mixture of isotopes, which are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons and so different mass numbers. Chlorine, for example, is about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. Because a real sample of an element contains a mixture of isotopes, chemists use an average mass for its atoms. This average is the relative atomic mass, symbol Ar. It is the value shown in the periodic table (usually the larger of the two numbers for each element).

The relative atomic mass is not a simple average of the mass numbers. It is a weighted average that takes account of how common (abundant) each isotope is. The percentage abundance of an isotope is the percentage of atoms of the element that are that isotope. The more abundant an isotope is, the closer the Ar is to its mass number. Chlorine's Ar is 35.5, much closer to 35 than to 37, because there are three times as many chlorine-35 atoms as chlorine-37 atoms.

To calculate Ar from percentage abundances: multiply the mass number of each isotope by its percentage abundance, add these together, and divide by 100. For chlorine: Ar = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 3550 ÷ 100 = 35.5. The same method works for elements with three or more isotopes: include a term for every isotope. Always check that the percentages add up to 100.

Relative atomic mass has no units because it is a relative value, comparing the masses of atoms with each other. Because it is an average, Ar is often not a whole number, even though every individual atom has a whole-number mass number. A useful check is that your answer must lie between the smallest and largest mass numbers of the isotopes, and nearer to the most abundant one.
keyFacts: Relative atomic mass (Ar) is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of an element.
Ar = (sum of mass number × percentage abundance for each isotope) ÷ 100.
Ar values are often not whole numbers because they are averages.
Ar is closest to the mass number of the most abundant isotope.
Percentage abundances of all isotopes of an element add up to 100%.
The Ar of each element is given in the periodic table.

keyTerms.definition: An average value of the mass of an element's atoms that takes account of the abundance of its isotopes.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The percentage of the atoms of an element that are a particular isotope.
An average in which each value counts in proportion to how common it is.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom of an isotope.

equations.name: Relative atomic mass from isotope abundances
equations.formula: Ar = (mass number of isotope 1 × % abundance of isotope 1 + mass number of isotope 2 × % abundance of isotope 2) ÷ 100, adding a term for every isotope

workedExamples.title: Two isotopes
workedExamples.question: Boron has two isotopes: boron-10 (20%) and boron-11 (80%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron.
steps: Multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance: 10 × 20 = 200 and 11 × 80 = 880.
Check: 10.8 lies between 10 and 11 and is nearer 11, the more abundant isotope.

workedExamples.title: Three isotopes
workedExamples.question: Magnesium is 79% magnesium-24, 10% magnesium-25 and 11% magnesium-26. Calculate the Ar of magnesium to 1 decimal place.
steps: Ar = 2432 ÷ 100 = 24.32, which is 24.3 to 1 decimal place.

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing abundance
workedExamples.question: Neon is 90.5% neon-20, 9.2% neon-22 and the rest is neon-21. What is the percentage abundance of neon-21?
steps: The abundances must add up to 100%.

workedExamples.title: Working backwards (Higher demand)
workedExamples.question: Copper has isotopes copper-63 and copper-65 and an Ar of 63.5. Calculate the percentage abundance of copper-63.
steps: Let the abundance of copper-63 be x%. Then copper-65 is (100 − x)%.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often find Ar by simply averaging the mass numbers, for example (35 + 37) ÷ 2 = 36 for chlorine.
misconceptions.right: In fact Ar is a weighted average: each mass number must be multiplied by its percentage abundance. For chlorine this gives 35.5.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an atom can have a mass number of 35.5.
misconceptions.right: In fact every individual atom has a whole-number mass number. 35.5 is the average for a large number of chlorine atoms.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often give Ar a unit such as grams.
misconceptions.right: In fact Ar is a relative value and has no units.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often forget to divide by 100 and give an answer like 3550.
misconceptions.right: In fact the answer must lie between the mass numbers of the isotopes. If it does not, check that you divided by 100.

realWorld: Ar values are used in every calculation of relative formula mass, such as working out how much product a chemical plant will make.
Scientists measure isotope abundances with a mass spectrometer, and small differences in abundance can reveal where a sample of food or a mineral came from.
Lead from different ore deposits has slightly different isotope abundances, so its Ar varies a little; this helps archaeologists trace ancient metal objects.
examTips: Show every multiplication, the total, and the division by 100. Method marks are available even if you make an arithmetic slip.
Check your answer is between the smallest and largest mass numbers and closest to the most abundant isotope.
Give answers to the number of decimal places asked for (often 1 decimal place).
If one percentage is missing, subtract the others from 100 first.
summary: Ar is an average mass that takes account of the abundance of each isotope.
Ar has no units and is often not a whole number.
Ar is closest to the mass number of the most abundant isotope.
Chlorine's Ar is 35.5 because it is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37.

questions.question: What is the relative atomic mass of an element?
options: The number of protons in an atom of the element
The mass number of the most common isotope
An average value that takes account of the abundance of the element's isotopes
The total number of protons, neutrons and electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: an average value that takes account of the abundance of the element's isotopes
questions.explanation: Ar is a weighted average of the isotopes' masses. The number of protons is the atomic number, and the most common isotope's mass number is only one of the values in the average.

questions.question: What is the symbol for relative atomic mass?
options: Mr
Ar
Z
n
questions.explanation: Ar is relative atomic mass. Mr is relative formula mass, used for compounds.

questions.question: Which information is needed to calculate the relative atomic mass of an element?
options: The mass number and percentage abundance of each isotope
The atomic number and the number of electrons
The number of neutrons in one atom
The melting point and density of the element
markScheme: 1 mark: the mass number and percentage abundance of each isotope
questions.explanation: Ar is calculated from each isotope's mass number weighted by its abundance.

questions.question: Why is the relative atomic mass of chlorine 35.5 and not a whole number?
options: Some chlorine atoms have half a neutron
Chlorine atoms lose electrons easily
Electrons add 0.5 to the mass
It is an average of the masses of chlorine's isotopes
markScheme: 1 mark: it is an average of the masses of chlorine's isotopes
questions.explanation: Individual atoms have whole-number mass numbers (35 or 37). The average of many atoms, weighted by abundance, is 35.5.

questions.question:
Element X has two isotopes.
Table 1 shows the abundance of each isotope.
What is the relative atomic mass of X?
questions.explanation: (79 × 50 + 81 × 50) ÷ 100 = 80. With equal abundances the weighted average is halfway between the two mass numbers.

questions.question: Boron has isotopes boron-10 and boron-11. Its relative atomic mass is 10.8. What does this tell you?
options: Boron-11 is more abundant than boron-10
Boron-10 is more abundant than boron-11
Both isotopes are equally abundant
Boron has a third isotope with a mass of 10.8
markScheme: 1 mark: boron-11 is more abundant than boron-10
questions.explanation: 10.8 is closer to 11 than to 10, so there must be more boron-11 atoms. Equal abundance would give 10.5.

questions.question: What are the units of relative atomic mass?
options: g
g/mol
amu per atom
It has no units
questions.explanation: Ar compares the masses of atoms with each other, so it is a ratio with no units.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of lithium.
What is the relative atomic mass of lithium to 1 decimal place?
questions.explanation: (6 × 7.5 + 7 × 92.5) ÷ 100 = (45 + 647.5) ÷ 100 = 6.925, which is 6.9 to 1 decimal place. 6.5 is the simple (unweighted) average.

questions.question: An element has two isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37. Its relative atomic mass is 35.5. What is the percentage abundance of the isotope with mass number 35?
questions.explanation: 35x + 37(100 − x) = 3550 gives 3700 − 2x = 3550, so x = 75. 25% is the abundance of the mass-37 isotope.

questions.question: Hydrogen has an isotope, deuterium (²H), but the relative atomic mass of hydrogen is 1.0 to 1 decimal place. What is the best explanation?
options: Deuterium has no neutrons
Deuterium has a very low percentage abundance
Ar only counts protons
Deuterium is a different element
markScheme: 1 mark: deuterium has a very low percentage abundance
questions.explanation: Almost all hydrogen atoms are ¹H, so the weighted average is very close to 1. Deuterium is hydrogen with one neutron, so it is the same element.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of copper.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: The answer is closer to 63 because copper-63 is more abundant.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of bromine.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of bromine.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: The two isotopes are almost equally abundant, so Ar is very close to 80, halfway between 79 and 81.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of neon.
Calculate the percentage abundance of neon-21.
questions.explanation: The percentage abundances of all the isotopes of an element add up to 100%.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of gallium.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of gallium.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: Multiply, add, divide by 100, then round to 1 decimal place.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the three isotopes of magnesium.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: With three isotopes, include a term for each. The answer lies between 24 and 26 and is closest to 24.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the three isotopes of silicon.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: Most silicon atoms are silicon-28, so Ar is only slightly above 28.

questions.question:
Copper has two isotopes, copper-63 and copper-65.
A sample of copper has a relative atomic mass of 63.5
Calculate the percentage abundance of copper-63 in this sample.
questions.explanation: Let x be the percentage of copper-63; the rest, 100 − x, is copper-65. Check: (63 × 75 + 65 × 25) ÷ 100 = (4725 + 1625) ÷ 100 = 63.5.

questions.question: What is meant by the relative atomic mass of an element?
markScheme: 1 mark: an average value (of the mass of the atoms of an element)
1 mark: that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element
questions.explanation: Both ideas are needed: an average, and weighting by the abundance of each isotope.

questions.question: What is meant by the percentage abundance of an isotope?
acceptedAnswers: proportion of atoms that are that isotope
markScheme: 1 mark: the percentage of the atoms of the element that are that isotope
questions.explanation: For example, 75% of chlorine atoms are chlorine-35.

questions.question: Explain why the relative atomic mass of chlorine (35.5) is closer to 35 than to 37.
markScheme: 1 mark: Ar is an average that takes account of abundance
1 mark: chlorine-35 is more abundant (75%) than chlorine-37 (25%)
questions.explanation: The more common isotope contributes more to the weighted average.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of boron.
A student calculates the relative atomic mass of boron as (10 + 11) ÷ 2 = 10.5
Explain the student's mistake and give the correct value.
acceptedAnswers: did not take account of abundance
markScheme: 1 mark: the student ignored the abundances / used a simple average, but the isotopes are not equally abundant

questions.question: Give one reason why relative atomic masses are often not whole numbers.
markScheme: 1 mark: Ar is an average of the masses of the different isotopes (weighted by abundance)
questions.explanation: Each atom has a whole-number mass number, but the average of a mixture of isotopes need not be whole.

questions.question: Potassium has isotopes potassium-39, potassium-40 and potassium-41. Its relative atomic mass is 39.1. Suggest which isotope is the most abundant and explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the Ar (39.1) is very close to 39, and Ar is closest to the mass number of the most abundant isotope
questions.explanation: If potassium-40 or potassium-41 were most abundant, the Ar would be well above 39.1.

questions.question: Copper has isotopes copper-63 and copper-65 and an Ar of 63.5. A student claims that most copper atoms are copper-65. Use the Ar to explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: if the isotopes were equally abundant the Ar would be 64
1 mark: 63.5 is below 64 / closer to 63, so copper-63 must be more abundant
questions.explanation: Comparing with the halfway value (64) shows which isotope dominates. The actual abundance of copper-63 is about 75%.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the isotopes of chlorine.
Describe how to calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the percentage abundances of its isotopes.
Use chlorine as an example.
markScheme: Indicative content: multiply the mass number of each isotope by its percentage abundance (35 × 75 = 2625; 37 × 25 = 925); add the results (3550); divide by 100 (35.5); Ar has no units; answer should be between the mass numbers and closest to the most abundant isotope.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear, correct method in the right order, with a fully worked chlorine example giving 35.5.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct steps or a correct answer without a clear method.
questions.explanation: The method is a weighted average: multiply, add, divide by 100.

questions.question:
Magnesium has three isotopes.
Table 1 shows the percentage abundance of each isotope.
Explain what is meant by isotopes and by relative atomic mass.
Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium.
Explain why the value is not a whole number and why it is closest to 24.
markScheme: Indicative content: isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons (12 for magnesium) but different numbers of neutrons (12, 13 and 14); relative atomic mass is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes; calculation: 24 × 79 = 1896, 25 × 10 = 250, 26 × 11 = 286; total 2432; ÷ 100 = 24.32 (24.3); not a whole number because it is an average of different isotope masses; closest to 24 because magnesium-24 is by far the most abundant (79%).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct definitions, a fully correct calculation with working, and clear explanations of both features of the answer.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct calculation with at least one correct definition or explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant statements or a partly correct calculation.
questions.explanation: The weighted average of 24.32 reflects the dominance of magnesium-24.
